subject: Reader mailbag: 5 questions investors actually ask
preheader: LLC structure · partnership splits · firing your PM · first-deal regrets · refi timing math

marketSnapshot.headline: The 5 questions every investor eventually asks
marketSnapshot.body: Some weeks the deal-spotter and the topic essay aren't the highlight — the inbox is. Five recurring questions investors ask after the first 1-3 deals. Each one is worth answering in detail because the answers compound over a portfolio. Reply to this email any time with a question and it might end up here in a future edition.

dealSpotter.body: Owner-occupants must take the loan in personal name (FHA, conventional). Pure investments can go in an LLC — but each LLC typically holds 2-4 properties for liability isolation. Don't put 10 properties in one LLC; if one tenant slip-and-falls, all 10 are in litigation. Don't put 1 property in 1 LLC each either — bookkeeping overhead is real. Sweet spot: 3-4 properties per LLC, geographic clustering matters.

dealSpotter.address: Q2: Partnership 60/40 split — who pays capex surprises?
dealSpotter.body: Capex contributions follow ownership percentage. If you're 60% and your partner is 40%, a $10k capex surprise is $6k from you and $4k from them. The trap: figuring this out AFTER the surprise. Write the operating agreement with explicit capex contribution rules before the deal closes. Include who decides what's 'maintenance' vs 'capex,' the reserve account funding mechanism, and the exit-from-partnership procedure if one party can't make a contribution.

dealSpotter.address: Q3: When to fire your property manager
dealSpotter.body: Five fire-the-PM triggers. (1) Vacancy materially above market — if local DOM is 30 days and your unit has been empty 45+, that's a slow placement. (2) Maintenance bills consistently 20%+ above local contractor pricing. (3) Tenant complaints routing TO YOU instead of being handled before they reach you. (4) Can't get a real answer within 48 hours on simple questions. (5) Missed a state-required compliance step. Document everything, give 30-60 days notice per most state laws, have the replacement PM lined up before terminating.

blogFeature.title: Property management yes or no — the actual math
blogFeature.excerpt: 8-10% of rent + lease-up fees + maintenance markup adds up to 13-18% of gross rent. The honest math on when self-management beats PM and vice-versa.

qa.question: Q4: First-deal regret — what would you do differently? Q5: Refi timing math — when does it actually work?
qa.answer: Q4: Almost every first-time investor over-pays by 5-10% and under-budgets capex by 30-50%. The lesson isn't to wait for a perfect first deal — it's to accept that the first deal will be your most-expensive education and not let perfect be the enemy of started. Run the deal in TrueCap with conservative assumptions (8% capex, 8% vacancy, 9% PM, 25% over-budget rehab). If it still pencils, buy. The deal that needs aggressive assumptions to pencil is the one that breaks you. Q5: Refi math has two parts. The savings: monthly P&I difference between current rate and refi rate, times months held post-refi. The cost: closing costs (typically $4-8k on a single-family) plus the time-value of the equity you don't extract. Break-even = closing costs ÷ monthly savings. If you'll hold past the break-even (typically 24-36 months), refi. If you'll sell or refi-again before break-even, skip. The other angle: cash-out refi while you're at it can fund the next deal — that compounds the math meaningfully and is often the real reason to refi at the borderline case.
